The abstract will summarize the core categories investigated: training-time data and model poisoning, inference-time adversarial attacks and prompt injection, and the intrinsic reliability challenges posed by LLM hallucinations. The discussion will begin with early efforts focusing on simple fine-tuning vulnerabilities, such as exposing Personally Identifiable Information (PII) through minimal poisoned instances, as noted in [Chowdhury_2024_Breaking]. It will then analyze sophisticated fine-tuning attacks, specifically highlighting [Yang_2024_Adversarial]'s exploration of QLoRA to inject domain-specific vulnerabilities in medical contexts (e.g., dropping safe vaccine recommendations to 2.49% while maintaining general benchmark performance). The section will emphasize the stealthy nature of these attacks and the paradigm shift required to address open-ended text generation backdoors compared to traditional classification backdoors.

outline.description: Focusing on the 2024-2026 timeline, this section examines the evolution of adversarial attacks in LLMs and MLLMs. It will document the shift from localized, modality-specific vulnerabilities toward highly sophisticated, transferable threats. The section will deeply analyze query-based black-box attacks, using [Wang_2024_Advqdet] as a primary case study to illustrate early targeted attack vectors and the corresponding development of stateful detection mechanisms utilizing Adversarial Contrastive Prompt Tuning on CLIP embeddings. It will discuss how attackers exploit the high-dimensional embedding spaces of multimodal models to bypass safety alignments, and how these attacks have scaled in complexity, necessitating massive-scale, systemic benchmarking.

outline.title: Inference-Time Threats II: Prompt Injection and Agentic Vulnerabilities
outline.description: This section covers the rapid evolution of Prompt Injection, culminating in the highly sophisticated paradigms of the 2025 literature. It will trace the trajectory from early static, single-turn manual attacks designed to bypass basic safety filters, to the current era of dynamic, agentic, and co-evolutionary adversarial dynamics. Key focus areas will include the automation of adaptive, search-based attacks and the critical shift toward Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI) in autonomous LLM agents. The section will explain how the integration of LLMs into complex, tool-using systems has rendered static heuristic defenses brittle, creating a landscape where adversaries and models co-evolve in real-time.

outline.title: Model Reliability and Trust: LLM Hallucinations
outline.description: Framing hallucinations as a critical security and reliability vulnerability, this section details the profound maturation in theoretical understanding and methodological sophistication between 2023 and 2025. It will contrast the early normative view of hallucinations as strict errors with more recent theoretical reframings. The narrative will begin with the foundational work of [Friel_2023_LLM], discussing the use of Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting to elicit boolean judgments and human-readable justifications. It will then transition to the 2024 bifurcation of research into theoretical reframing and the engineering of scalable annotation systems, highlighting [Gu_2024_Anah]'s iterative approach to overcoming the prohibitive labor costs and unreliability of proprietary APIs like GPT-4 for fine-grained hallucination annotation.

outline.title: Cross-Cutting Defenses and Mitigation Strategies
outline.description: This section provides a holistic overview of defense mechanisms across the various threat categories, tracing the evolution from static to dynamic defenses. It will discuss the brittleness of early static prompt engineering, simple perplexity checks, and basic instruction filtering against modern attacks. The section will highlight advanced, localized defense mechanisms like the stateful detection utilizing Adversarial Contrastive Prompt Tuning on CLIP embeddings [Wang_2024_Advqdet]. Furthermore, it will explore the rise of dynamic, co-evolutionary defense mechanisms designed to counter automated adaptive attacks and Indirect Prompt Injections in agentic workflows, proposing a unified defense architecture for future LLM deployments.

outline.title: Testing Methodologies and Evaluation
outline.description: This MANDATORY dedicated section synthesizes the evaluation frameworks, benchmarks, datasets, and metrics across ALL threat categories, highlighting the critical need for massive-scale, systemic benchmarking. It will discuss the inadequacy of older evaluation datasets (e.g., SummEval, QAGS) that relied on weaker models, as noted in hallucination research [Friel_2023_LLM]. It will detail the shift toward standardized benchmarking frameworks for open-ended text generation, prominently featuring BackdoorLLM [Li_2024_Backdoorllm] for poisoning evaluation. The section will also cover the evolution of metrics, from basic Adherence and Correctness to complex automated evaluations using LLMs as judges, while critically addressing the limitations and unreliability of using proprietary APIs (like GPT-4) as ground-truth evaluators [Gu_2024_Anah].

outline.title: Discussion and Open Challenges
outline.description: This section critically analyzes the gaps, limitations, and future directions in LLM security research. It will address the escalating threat of multi-modal vulnerabilities and the challenges of securing autonomous, tool-using LLM agents against Indirect Prompt Injection. The discussion will emphasize the ongoing arms race between automated attack generation and dynamic defenses. Furthermore, it will highlight the critical open challenge of evaluation bottlenecks, specifically the over-reliance on proprietary, opaque APIs for benchmarking, and the urgent need for open, massive-scale, systemic benchmarking frameworks that can keep pace with rapid model evolution.

outline.title: Conclusion
outline.description: The conclusion synthesizes the core findings of the survey, reiterating the profound shift in the LLM security landscape from static, isolated vulnerabilities to dynamic, systemic, and agentic threats. It will provide actionable, practical recommendations for researchers and practitioners, emphasizing the necessity of integrating security at both the training (anti-poisoning) and inference (dynamic filtering, stateful detection) stages. The section will close with a forward-looking statement on the imperative of collaborative, open-source benchmarking to ensure the safe deployment of next-generation generative models.

introduction.title: Introduction
introduction.text:
# Introduction

### 1. Motivation
The emergence of artificial intelligence has marked a significant transformation in Natural Language Processing (NLP) through the introduction of Large Language Models (LLMs). These models have enabled unprecedented advances in language comprehension, generation, and translation, becoming a cornerstone in both academic research and commercial applications [Chowdhury_2024_Breaking]. By leveraging massive datasets and advanced neural architectures, LLMs exhibit remarkable performance across diverse applications, increasingly acting as autonomous agents that use external tools to interact with complex environments [Zhan_2025_LLM]. However, with their rising prominence and integration into critical societal infrastructure, the security and vulnerability aspects of these models have garnered significant attention [Chowdhury_2024_Breaking].

Ensuring LLM alignment is critical to information security as AI models become increasingly widespread [Zhang_2025_Real]. Despite their transformative impact, LLMs are susceptible to a myriad of adversarial threats. Malicious actors can exploit these models to generate harmful content, leak sensitive information, or execute unauthorized actions. The integration of external tools further exacerbates these risks, introducing vulnerabilities such as indirect prompt injection (IPI) attacks [Zhan_2025_LLM]. Furthermore, research indicates that standard fine-tuning procedures may inadvertently weaken a model's safety alignment, thereby increasing its vulnerability to sophisticated exploits like backdoor jailbreaking attacks [Li_2024_Backdoorllm]. Therefore, understanding these vulnerabilities is imperative for ensuring the security, safety, and trustworthiness of AI-driven systems [Chowdhury_2024_Breaking]. The motivation for this survey stems from the urgent need to consolidate the fragmented knowledge surrounding LLM security, providing researchers and practitioners with a clear understanding of the evolving threat landscape and the efficacy of current defense mechanisms.

### 2. Scope of Survey
This survey provides a comprehensive overview of the security landscape surrounding Large Language Models, specifically focusing on the adversarial attacks targeting these systems and the corresponding defensive strategies developed to mitigate them. The scope of this paper encompasses a wide spectrum of vulnerabilities, ranging from foundational issues in base models to complex attack vectors in LLM-integrated agents. We systematically categorize the LLM attacks literature into a novel taxonomy to provide a better structure and aid for future research [Chowdhury_2024_Breaking]. This taxonomy classifies threats based on the adversary's access to model weights (white-box versus black-box) and the specific attack vectors employed, such as prompt injection, jailbreaking, and data poisoning.

While research on LLM safety predates the focus on LLM agent safety, our survey covers both domains. We examine how base LLMs, trained on large web corpora, are aligned using methods like Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) to prevent the generation of toxic or biased content [Zhan_2025_LLM]. Concurrently, we extend our analysis to the unique challenges posed by LLM agents, where the integration of external tools introduces new attack surfaces. The survey critically evaluates various defense mechanisms, noting that many current defenses against adversarial attacks and jailbreaking cannot adapt quickly to new threats, often degrade model responses to benign prompts, or introduce significant barriers to scalable implementation [Zhang_2025_Real]. By delineating the boundaries between different types of attacks—such as the empirical discrepancy in defense performance between backdoor refusal and jailbreaking tasks [Li_2024_Backdoorllm]—this survey aims to provide a nuanced understanding of what current security measures can and cannot achieve.

### 3. Temporal Trends (2023-2026)
The landscape of LLM security has evolved rapidly, characterized by a continuous arms race between attackers and defenders. Analyzing the temporal trends from 2023 to 2026 reveals a distinct trajectory in the sophistication of both threats and mitigations.

In **2023**, the widespread public release of highly capable LLMs led to the initial discovery of basic jailbreaks and direct prompt injections. The primary focus of the research community during this period was on base model alignment, heavily relying on RLHF and supervised fine-tuning to instill basic safety guardrails [Zhan_2025_LLM]. However, these early defenses were often brittle and easily bypassed by heuristic-based adversarial prompts.

Moving into **2024**, the threat landscape matured significantly. Attackers began exploiting the fine-tuning process itself, demonstrating that customized fine-tuning could inadvertently degrade safety alignment and open the door to backdoor jailbreaking attacks [Li_2024_Backdoorllm]. Furthermore, as LLMs transitioned from passive text generators to active agents, 2024 saw a surge in research concerning indirect prompt injections (IPI), where malicious instructions are embedded in external data sources accessed by the LLM [Zhan_2025_LLM]. The literature from this year highlights a growing realization that static defenses are insufficient against dynamic, multi-step agentic workflows.

In **2025**, the focus has shifted towards real-time, adaptive defenses and the scalable implementation of security measures. Researchers are grappling with the reality that many existing defenses degrade the utility of the model or fail to generalize to novel attack variants [Zhang_2025_Real]. There is a pronounced emphasis on developing robust alignment techniques that maintain efficacy even when subjected to adversarial fine-tuning or complex jailbreak-style triggers, which have proven notoriously difficult to defend against compared to simple refusal-style backdoors [Li_2024_Backdoorllm].

Projecting into **2026**, we anticipate a paradigm shift towards provable security and autonomous defense mechanisms. As LLM agents become deeply embedded in critical infrastructure, the demand for formal verification of LLM behaviors will rise. We expect to see the emergence of standardized, dynamic benchmarking frameworks that continuously evaluate adversarial robustness, moving away from static datasets. Additionally, 2026 will likely witness the integration of neuro-symbolic approaches to enforce hard security constraints that cannot be unlearned during subsequent fine-tuning phases.

### 4. Contributions
In light of the rapidly shifting threat landscape and the critical need for robust AI systems, this survey makes several key contributions to the field of LLM security:

First, we present a comprehensive and up-to-date taxonomy of attacks targeting Large Language Models. By categorizing the spectrum of attacks based on access levels and attack vectors, we provide a structured framework that clarifies the distinct challenges associated with each threat type [Chowdhury_2024_Breaking]. This taxonomy serves as a foundational tool for researchers to systematically navigate the complex literature on LLM vulnerabilities.

Second, we provide an in-depth analysis of the temporal evolution of LLM security from 2023 to 2026. By tracing the trajectory from basic prompt injections to sophisticated agentic exploits and backdoor vulnerabilities, we highlight the dynamic nature of the arms race between attackers and defenders. This historical and predictive perspective offers valuable insights into where the field is heading and what future challenges must be anticipated.

Third, we critically evaluate the efficacy and limitations of state-of-the-art defense mechanisms. We synthesize empirical findings that reveal critical discrepancies in defense performance, such as the stark contrast in effectiveness when mitigating refusal-style backdoors versus jailbreak-style triggers [Li_2024_Backdoorllm]. Furthermore, we address the practical challenges of implementing these defenses, emphasizing the trade-offs between security, model utility, and scalability [Zhang_2025_Real].

Finally, we identify critical gaps in the current research and propose a roadmap for future investigations. By highlighting the inadequacies of current defenses against indirect prompt injections in LLM agents [Zhan_2025_LLM] and the degradation of alignment during fine-tuning, we outline actionable research directions aimed at developing more resilient, adaptive, and provably secure AI systems. Through these contributions, this survey endeavors to equip the research community with the knowledge necessary to build the next generation of trustworthy Large Language Models.

background_and_preliminaries.text:
# Background and Preliminaries

**LLM Architecture Basics**
Large Language Models (LLMs) have fundamentally transformed Natural Language Processing (NLP) by demonstrating unprecedented capabilities in understanding, generating, and reasoning with human-like text [Chowdhury_2024_Breaking]. At the core of these models lies the Transformer architecture, a paradigm-shifting design that relies heavily on the self-attention mechanism. Unlike earlier recurrent neural networks (RNNs) that processed data sequentially, Transformers process tokens in parallel. This parallelization not only enables highly efficient training on modern GPU clusters but also allows the model to capture long-range dependencies and complex contextual relationships across vast sequences of text. The self-attention mechanism computes a weighted representation of all tokens in a sequence for each given token, effectively determining which parts of the input are most relevant to the current context. Furthermore, because Transformers lack an inherent sense of sequence order, positional encodings are injected into the input embeddings to provide the model with information about the relative or absolute position of each token.

The development of a modern LLM typically follows a rigorous, multi-stage pipeline. The foundational stage is pre-training, where the model is exposed to massive, diverse corpora of text data, often comprising trillions of tokens scraped from the internet, books, and articles. During this unsupervised phase, the model learns to predict the next token in a sequence. Through this simple objective, the model acquires a broad understanding of grammar, facts, reasoning abilities, and world knowledge. However, because base LLMs are trained on unfiltered web corpora, they can inadvertently learn and generate harmful, toxic, or biased content [Zhan_2025_LLM].

To transform a base model into a useful and safe assistant, subsequent refinement stages are necessary. Following pre-training, the model undergoes Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), where it is trained on high-quality, human-annotated instruction-response pairs. This stage teaches the model to follow specific instructions, answer questions directly, and format its outputs appropriately. However, SFT alone is often insufficient to ensure the model behaves safely and aligns with complex human values. To address this, alignment techniques such as Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) are heavily employed [Zhan_2025_LLM]. In the RLHF framework, a separate reward model is first trained on human preference data to score the quality, helpfulness, and safety of the LLM's responses. The LLM is then optimized using reinforcement learning algorithms, such as Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), to maximize this reward signal [Duan_2025_RLHF]. While these stages—pre-training, SFT, and alignment—are critical for producing capable models, they also introduce distinct attack surfaces that adversaries can exploit throughout the model's lifecycle [Duan_2025_RLHF].

**Threat Taxonomy**
As LLMs become increasingly integrated into critical applications—ranging from healthcare and finance to software development and customer service—their security and vulnerability aspects have garnered significant attention. This necessitates a comprehensive threat taxonomy to structure the understanding of these risks and guide future research [Chowdhury_2024_Breaking]. The threat landscape for LLMs is highly diverse, encompassing vulnerabilities that span the entire model lifecycle, from initial data collection to real-world deployment.

A primary category in this taxonomy is Data and Model Poisoning. In these attacks, adversaries manipulate the data used during the pre-training, SFT, or RLHF stages. By injecting maliciously crafted examples into the training corpus, attackers can embed hidden backdoors or alter the model's behavior in specific, targeted ways [Li_2024_Backdoorllm]. For instance, poisoning preference data during the RLHF stage can compromise the reward model, leading the LLM to generate harmful or misaligned content when a specific trigger phrase is presented [Duan_2025_RLHF]. Because LLMs require massive datasets, ensuring the cryptographic integrity and provenance of all training data is a monumental challenge, making poisoning a persistent threat.

Another critical category is Adversarial Attacks, which involve crafting inputs designed to deceive the model into making errors, hallucinating, or bypassing safety filters. These attacks range from human-crafted, heuristic-based manipulations—which are often slow and non-scalable—to automated methods that utilize search algorithms, target function optimization, and even other LLMs to generate adversarial prompts [Chowdhury_2024_Breaking].

Prompt Injection and Jailbreaking form a highly visible subset of adversarial attacks specifically tailored to instruction-following LLMs. In direct prompt injection, attackers embed malicious instructions within the user input, overriding the model's original system prompts and constraints. Indirect prompt injection occurs when an LLM processes external, attacker-controlled data (e.g., summarizing a malicious webpage), which then hijacks the model's context. These attacks can lead to unauthorized actions, data exfiltration, or the generation of prohibited content.

Furthermore, the taxonomy includes threats related to Privacy and Data Extraction. Because LLMs have a tendency to memorize portions of their training data, attackers can craft specific queries to extract sensitive, personally identifiable information (PII), copyrighted material, or proprietary data that the model was exposed to during pre-training. Understanding this multifaceted taxonomy is essential for developing robust mitigation strategies and ensuring the secure deployment of LLMs [Chowdhury_2024_Breaking].

**Attacker Capabilities**
To accurately assess the risks posed by the threats outlined in the taxonomy, it is crucial to define the capabilities of potential attackers. The threat model for LLMs varies significantly based on the attacker's level of access, computational resources, and ultimate objectives.

At the most privileged level, attackers may have the capability to intervene directly in the model's training process. This includes the ability to manipulate the training data, modify model parameters, or influence the training algorithms [Li_2024_Backdoorllm]. Such capabilities are often assumed in data poisoning and weight poisoning scenarios. For example, an attacker might compromise a data source routinely scraped during pre-training, or contribute malicious instruction-tuning datasets to popular open-source repositories. In more sophisticated attacks, adversaries might manipulate hidden states or hijack the chain-of-thought reasoning processes of the model during fine-tuning [Li_2024_Backdoorllm]. This level of access is typically associated with insider threats, compromised supply chains, or malicious data providers.

In deployment scenarios, attacker capabilities are often defined by their interaction with the system as end-users or API consumers. A common threat model in this context is the "Content-Author Attack," where a malicious actor submits text containing adversarial elements designed to manipulate the model's assessment or output [Maloyan_2025_LLM]. In this scenario, the submitted text passes through the evaluation pipeline unchanged, allowing the attacker to exploit vulnerabilities in how the LLM processes and interprets the input [Maloyan_2025_LLM]. This is particularly relevant for LLMs used as judges, evaluators, or content moderators.

Attackers can also be categorized by their computational resources and adaptability. Resource-constrained attackers may rely on manual prompt engineering, social engineering, or basic black-box querying to find vulnerabilities. In contrast, well-resourced attackers—such as state-sponsored actors or organized cybercriminal groups—might employ automated optimization techniques, leverage massive compute clusters to train surrogate models for transferable adversarial examples, or conduct large-scale, coordinated data poisoning campaigns. Furthermore, modern threat models must account for adaptive attackers who actively modify their strategies in response to deployed defenses, continuously probing for new vulnerabilities as the system evolves. 

**Black-box vs. White-box**
Within the context of adversarial attacks and model evaluation, threat models are broadly classified into distinct paradigms based on the attacker's knowledge of and access to the target system. The two primary classifications are white-box and black-box attacks, though gray-box scenarios also exist as an intermediate threat model.

White-box attacks assume the adversary has complete and transparent access to the target LLM. This includes full knowledge of the model's architecture, training data, algorithms, weights, gradients, and hyperparameters [Chowdhury_2024_Breaking]. With this level of access, attackers can employ sophisticated, gradient-based optimization techniques to craft highly effective adversarial examples. By calculating the exact gradient of the loss function with respect to the input tokens, attackers can systematically perturb the input to maximize the model's error or force it to generate specific malicious outputs. White-box access also permits deep analysis of the model's internal representations, enabling attacks that manipulate hidden states or extract sensitive information with high precision [Chowdhury_2024_Breaking]. While white-box scenarios represent the worst-case security threat, they are less common in practice for proprietary, closed-source models (e.g., OpenAI's GPT-4 or Anthropic's Claude). However, they are highly relevant and critical for the security analysis of open-weight models, where the model parameters are publicly available.

Conversely, black-box attacks operate under the assumption that the attacker has limited or no knowledge of the model's internal workings. In these scenarios, the adversary can only interact with the LLM through its input-output interface, typically via an API or a web-based user interface [Chowdhury_2024_Breaking]. The attacker submits prompts and observes the generated responses, without any access to gradients, weights, or internal states. Black-box attacks are highly realistic and represent the most common and immediate threat to deployed commercial LLMs. To execute these attacks, adversaries often rely on transferability—crafting adversarial examples on a local, accessible surrogate model (a white-box environment) and transferring them to the target black-box model, hoping the vulnerability generalizes across architectures. Alternatively, they may use query-based optimization methods, such as evolutionary algorithms or reinforcement learning, to iteratively refine their inputs based solely on the model's text outputs. Despite the restricted access, black-box attacks pose severe risks, including sensitive data extraction, the generation of biased or harmful outputs, and the circumvention of safety guardrails, ultimately diminishing trust in AI systems [Chowdhury_2024_Breaking].

Between these extremes lie gray-box attacks, where the attacker possesses partial knowledge of the system. For instance, an attacker might know the model architecture and the defense mechanisms in place, but lack access to the specific weights or training data. Alternatively, they might have access to the model's confidence scores or output logits via an API, but not the underlying gradients. Gray-box models provide a nuanced and highly practical framework for evaluating the security of systems that expose more than just text outputs but remain fundamentally closed-source.

# Training-Time Threats: Data and Model Poisoning

The rapid evolution of Large Language Models (LLMs) and multimodal artificial intelligence systems has fundamentally shifted the machine learning landscape toward a complex, multi-stage paradigm: massive-scale pre-training followed by task-specific fine-tuning and human-centric alignment `[Chowdhury_2024_Breaking]`. While this layered approach democratizes access to high-performing models and allows for rapid adaptation to specialized domains, it simultaneously introduces a vast and highly vulnerable attack surface during the training phases. Training-time threats represent a critical category of security vulnerabilities where adversaries intentionally manipulate the training data, the fine-tuning process, or the model weights themselves. The goal is to embed malicious behaviors, extract sensitive information, or degrade overall performance. Unlike inference-time attacks—such as prompt injection or jailbreaking, which attempt to subvert a frozen model—training-time threats are deeply insidious. They alter the foundational behavior and latent representations of the model, often remaining entirely dormant until triggered by specific, adversary-defined conditions. This section explores the multifaceted landscape of training-time threats, specifically focusing on the mechanics of data poisoning, direct model poisoning, the unique vulnerabilities introduced by parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods like QLoRA, the critical risk of Personally Identifiable Information (PII) exposure, and the emergence of highly stealthy, clean-label attack vectors.

### Data Poisoning
Data poisoning constitutes one of the most pervasive and historically established training-time threats, exploiting the modern AI ecosystem's reliance on massive, often uncurated datasets. Because foundational models require petabytes of data, organizations frequently resort to scraping the public internet or crowdsourcing data from third-party annotators, making rigorous quality control nearly impossible. In a data poisoning attack, an adversary intentionally injects corrupted, mislabeled, or maliciously crafted examples into the training corpus to manipulate the model's learned representations. 

As models have evolved to incorporate complex alignment pipelines, the vectors for data poisoning have expanded accordingly. For instance, in text-to-image (T2I) models and LLMs, data poisoning can occur during two critical stages: the Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) stage and the Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) stage `[Duan_2025_RLHF]`. During the SFT stage, adversaries can directly manipulate the training data by injecting poisoned text-image pairs or prompt-response pairs into the dataset. Because SFT datasets are typically much smaller and more heavily weighted by the model during fine-tuning than the broad pre-training corpus, even a minuscule fraction of poisoned data can significantly skew the model's outputs and embed reliable backdoors.

Furthermore, the RLHF stage introduces entirely new, highly sensitive vulnerabilities. RLHF relies on training a reward model based on human preference data, which is subsequently used to optimize the primary generative model. Adversaries can execute poisoning attacks by manipulating this preference data—altering the ranking of responses to favor harmful, biased, or adversary-specified outputs `[Duan_2025_RLHF]`. By compromising the reward model, the attacker effectively hijacks the entire alignment process. This allows them to steer the model's generation toward malicious objectives even if the underlying SFT data remains pristine. The distributed and often outsourced nature of preference data collection makes it particularly susceptible to coordinated poisoning campaigns, highlighting a severe structural weakness in contemporary AI alignment methodologies.

### Model Poisoning
While data poisoning focuses on corrupting the input corpus, model poisoning involves more direct interventions in the training process, the fine-tuning algorithms, or the model weights themselves to embed vulnerabilities. Generative LLMs have achieved state-of-the-art results across numerous domains, yet they remain highly susceptible to backdoor attacks, where carefully crafted triggers in the input manipulate the model to produce adversary-specified outputs `[Li_2024_Badedit]`. Historically, mainstream backdoor attack methods demanded substantial tuning data and extensive computational resources to successfully poison a model. This requirement limited their practicality for resource-constrained attackers and often degraded the overall performance of the LLM on benign tasks, making the tampering easier to detect.

However, recent advancements have drastically lowered the barrier to entry for model poisoning. Attackers can now formulate backdoor injection as a lightweight knowledge editing problem `[Li_2024_Badedit]`. By treating the backdoor trigger as a specific "fact" or "rule" to be surgically edited into the model's parameters, adversaries can implant robust backdoors without the need for massive poisoned datasets or full-scale retraining. This targeted manipulation alters specific pathways within the neural network, ensuring that the model behaves perfectly normally under standard conditions but reliably executes the malicious payload when the trigger is present. 

Furthermore, the increasing trend of AI providers enabling end-users to fine-tune models via APIs enhances adaptability but also opens the door for users to intentionally or inadvertently poison models `[Chowdhury_2024_Breaking]`. If a compromised, fine-tuned model is shared publicly on open-source repositories (such as Hugging Face), it acts as a Trojan horse. Downstream developers who integrate these poisoned models into their applications unknowingly propagate the malicious weights, leading to widespread supply chain compromises.

### QLoRA Vulnerabilities
The democratization of LLM fine-tuning has been largely driven by Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) methods, with Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation (QLoRA) being one of the most prominent and widely adopted. QLoRA allows developers to fine-tune massive, state-of-the-art models on standard consumer-grade hardware by heavily quantizing the base model weights and training only a small set of low-rank adapter matrices. However, the very efficiency, low cost, and accessibility that make QLoRA revolutionary also introduce severe security vulnerabilities. Because QLoRA enables rapid fine-tuning, it significantly reduces the financial and computational resources required for an adversary to execute sophisticated fine-tuning attacks.

Research has explicitly demonstrated the vulnerability of both proprietary and open-source LLMs to fine-tuning adversarial attacks across critical, high-stakes domains, such as healthcare `[Yang_2024_Adversarial]`. In delicate medical contexts—such as vaccination guidance, medication prescribing, and diagnostic test recommendations—adversaries can use methods like QLoRA to subtly fine-tune a model to output harmful, biased, or scientifically inaccurate medical advice. Notably, forensic analysis reveals that the weights of models attacked via fine-tuning often exhibit a larger norm, which serves as a potential strategy for mitigating and detecting such attacks in future research `[Yang_2024_Adversarial]`. 

The modular nature of LoRA and QLoRA adapters exacerbates this threat. Because adapters are lightweight files that are loaded on top of a base model, malicious actors can easily train and distribute "poisoned adapters" disguised as helpful domain-specific upgrades. Unsuspecting users who download and apply these adapters to their clean base models will instantly inherit the adversarial behavior. This plug-and-play vulnerability necessitates robust security safeguards, rigorous provenance tracking, and cryptographic adapter scanning mechanisms in LLM deployment to protect against parameter-efficient poisoning attacks.

### PII Exposure
Beyond the injection of malicious behaviors and backdoors, training-time interventions—particularly fine-tuning—pose a severe and immediate threat to data privacy and the protection of Personally Identifiable Information (PII). During the massive pre-training phase, LLMs ingest vast quantities of internet data, inevitably memorizing sensitive information such as names, physical addresses, phone numbers, financial details, and email addresses. While safety alignment and RLHF are typically employed by model providers to prevent the model from divulging this memorized PII during inference, fine-tuning can inadvertently or maliciously break these fragile safety guardrails.

Contemporary NLP systems rely heavily on fine-tuning to tailor models for specific tasks, but recent analyses have shown that fine-tuning is significantly more effective than prompt engineering alone for inducing PII leakage `[Chowdhury_2024_Breaking]`. In targeted experiments exposing hundreds of target PIIs, researchers found that larger models trained on real-world data possess incredibly strong memorization capabilities. More alarmingly, even minimal fine-tuning can shift an LLM from a state of strict non-disclosure to revealing significant amounts of sensitive information `[Chowdhury_2024_Breaking]`. 

An adversary with fine-tuning access can intentionally train the model on a small, carefully crafted dataset designed to unlearn its privacy alignments, effectively "jailbreaking" the model at the weight level to extract PII. Conversely, benign users fine-tuning a model on their own proprietary data might accidentally degrade the model's global privacy safeguards through catastrophic forgetting, leading to unintended data leaks. This vulnerability underscores the fragility of current safety alignments and highlights the critical need for privacy-preserving fine-tuning techniques, such as Differential Privacy (DP), to ensure that the adaptation process does not resurrect and expose memorized pre-training data.

### Stealthy Attacks
As the awareness of data and model poisoning grows, AI defenders have developed increasingly sophisticated sanitization, auditing, and anomaly detection techniques to filter out malicious training examples. In response, adversaries have evolved their methodologies to execute highly stealthy attacks that easily evade standard defensive filters and human oversight. One of the most dangerous manifestations of this trend is the "clean-label" poisoning attack. Unlike traditional poisoning, where the input data is clearly mislabeled, visibly corrupted, or contains nonsensical trigger words, clean-label attacks utilize natural-appearing examples that perfectly match their assigned labels or preference annotations. This makes them virtually indistinguishable from benign data to human reviewers or automated data-quality scripts.

A prime example of this stealthy paradigm is the BADREWARD attack, a novel clean-label poisoning technique that exploits vulnerabilities in multi-modal RLHF pipelines for T2I models `[Duan_2025_RLHF]`. By inducing visual feature collisions in CLIP-based reward models, this method corrupts the reward signals without altering the underlying preference annotations `[Duan_2025_RLHF]`. To a human evaluator auditing the dataset, the preference data appears entirely correct, contextually appropriate, and benign. However, in the latent, high-dimensional space of the reward model, the poisoned examples mathematically collide with target features, enabling the adversary to steer the generation process toward harmful or specific outcomes. 

These stealthy attacks represent a profound challenge for AI security. Because they bypass traditional data auditing, they require deep semantic analysis of the model's latent representations to detect. The demonstrated feasibility of hijacking complex models by poisoning only a small fraction of data with natural-appearing examples emphasizes the urgent need for robust, representation-aware defenses in the AI training pipeline `[Duan_2025_RLHF]`. As models become more capable, the arms race between stealthy training-time attacks and defensive auditing mechanisms will remain a defining challenge in securing the next generation of artificial intelligence.

inference_time_threats_adversarial.title: Inference-Time Threats I: Adversarial Attacks and Jailbreaks
inference_time_threats_adversarial.text:
### Inference-Time Threats I: Adversarial Attacks and Jailbreaks

As Large Language Models (LLMs) transition from controlled research environments into widespread commercial and societal integration, their security posture at the point of deployment becomes a paramount concern. While training-time vulnerabilities—such as data poisoning and backdoor injection—require adversaries to have access to the data pipeline or the model weights, inference-time threats represent a more immediate and accessible attack vector. At inference time, the adversary interacts with the frozen, deployed model, attempting to manipulate its inputs to elicit unintended, harmful, or unauthorized outputs. This section provides a comprehensive examination of the primary methodologies employed by malicious actors to subvert LLM safeguards during operation. We explore the foundational concepts of adversarial attacks, the specific mechanics of jailbreaks designed to bypass alignment training, the practical realities of query-based black-box attacks, the pervasive danger of transferable threats, and the emerging attack surface introduced by multimodal vulnerabilities.

#### Adversarial Attacks

Adversarial attacks in the context of Large Language Models involve the deliberate crafting of input perturbations designed to cause the model to behave in a manner contrary to its intended design or safety guidelines. Unlike traditional software exploits that target code vulnerabilities, adversarial attacks exploit the statistical and geometric properties of the model's learned representation space. The integration of LLMs into high-stakes domains, such as healthcare, underscores the critical nature of these vulnerabilities. For instance, the susceptibility of LLMs to adversarial attacks poses a significant threat in medical diagnostics and treatment recommendations, where manipulated outputs could lead to harmful outcomes in delicate medical contexts [Yang_2024_Adversarial]. Attackers can employ relatively simple yet highly effective strategies to significantly alter a model's operational behavior within specific tasks, potentially allowing malicious entities to manipulate medical advice or pharmaceutical information [Yang_2024_Adversarial].

Beyond simple prompt manipulation, sophisticated optimization-based techniques have been developed to systematically generate adversarial inputs. Methods such as the Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG) algorithm demonstrate the ability to find discrete token sequences that, when appended to a malicious prompt as an adversarial suffix or prefix, force the model to comply with the attacker's instructions [Zhan_2025_LLM]. In the context of LLM agents—systems that utilize external tools and APIs to interact with environments—these attacks frequently manifest as Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI). Here, the adversarial payload is hidden within external content (e.g., a webpage the agent is instructed to summarize), causing the agent to execute unauthorized actions on behalf of the user [Zhan_2025_LLM]. The constant iteration of LLMs and their incorporation into alignment-critical applications, such as autonomous robotics and scientific research, creates an urgent necessity for maintaining continual safety against these evolving adversarial strategies [Zhang_2025_Real]. Developing robust defenses requires not only addressing existing attack vectors but also anticipating adaptive attacks designed specifically to circumvent newly implemented security measures [Zhan_2025_LLM].

#### Jailbreaks

While the term "adversarial attack" broadly encompasses any input designed to cause model failure, "jailbreaking" refers specifically to techniques aimed at bypassing the safety filters, ethical guardrails, and alignment training (such as Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback, or RLHF) that developers implement to prevent the generation of toxic, illegal, or harmful content. Jailbreak attacks exploit the inherent tension between a model's objective to be helpful and its objective to be harmless, detailing strategies to exploit model vulnerabilities for unauthorized actions and underscoring the critical need for robust defense mechanisms [Chowdhury_2024_Breaking].

The mechanics of jailbreaking often involve complex role-playing scenarios, hypothetical framing, or the use of specialized encoding to obfuscate the malicious intent of the prompt from the model's safety classifiers. Furthermore, the lifecycle of LLM deployment often involves fine-tuning base models for specific downstream tasks. Research indicates that these fine-tuning procedures may inadvertently weaken the model's safety alignment, thereby significantly increasing its vulnerability to backdoor jailbreaking attacks [Li_2024_Backdoorllm]. In targeted refusal tasks, where a model is expected to emit a predefined refusal message when a malicious trigger is detected, compromised models exhibit stark contrasts in behavior, with attack success rates (ASR) frequently exceeding 80% or 90% on architectures like LLaMA-2-13B [Li_2024_Backdoorllm].

Defending against jailbreaks is notoriously difficult. Many current defenses against adversarial attacks and jailbreaking on LLMs cannot adapt quickly to new, zero-day attacks [Zhang_2025_Real]. Furthermore, overly aggressive safety filters often degrade model responses to benign prompts—a phenomenon known as the "alignment tax"—or introduce significant computational barriers that hinder scalable implementation in production environments [Zhang_2025_Real]. As a result, jailbreaking remains a dynamic and highly active area of adversarial research, with attackers continuously finding novel semantic structures to bypass static defense mechanisms.

#### Query-based Black-box Attacks

In most real-world deployment scenarios, such as commercial APIs, the adversary does not have access to the model's internal architecture, weights, or gradients. This necessitates the use of black-box attack strategies. Query-based black-box adversarial attacks estimate adversarial gradients or optimize inputs based solely on the returned probability vectors or text outputs of the target model over a sequence of queries [Wang_2024_Advqdet]. The adversary generates adversarial examples by making multiple queries to the model and iteratively using the model's returns to refine the adversarial perturbations [Wang_2024_Advqdet].

This iterative optimization process often requires launching hundreds or thousands of visually or semantically similar queries to the target model. To counter this, defenders can implement stateful detection frameworks motivated by the observation that query-based attacks produce anomalous patterns of similar sequential queries, which can be detected by robust feature extractors [Wang_2024_Advqdet]. However, attackers continually refine their methods to minimize query counts and evade detection. Refined query-based jailbreaking represents a strategic approach that utilizes a minimal number of queries to achieve the desired malicious output, thereby flying under the radar of rate-limiting and stateful monitoring systems [Chowdhury_2024_Breaking].

Advanced fuzzing frameworks have also been developed to automate the discovery of vulnerabilities in black-box systems. For example, frameworks like AGENTVIGIL systematically conduct indirect prompt injection attacks against black-box agents across various architectures and tasks. By combining high-quality prompt templates, adaptive seed scoring, and Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS)-based seed selection algorithms, these frameworks overcome the challenges posed by the black-box nature of commercial APIs and efficiently discover highly effective adversarial prompts [Wang_2025_LLM]. The success of these query-based methods highlights the fundamental vulnerability of exposing powerful models via interactive interfaces, where the interface itself becomes the attack vector.

#### Transferable Threats

A particularly insidious aspect of adversarial machine learning is the phenomenon of transferability. Transferable threats occur when an adversarial example crafted to deceive one model (the surrogate) successfully deceives a different, unseen model (the target). This property is highly advantageous for attackers operating in black-box settings, as they can utilize open-source models (where they have full white-box access to compute gradients) to generate adversarial prompts, and then deploy these prompts against closed-source, proprietary models.

Research has demonstrated that adversarial frameworks can be effectively transferred across a wide variety of LLMs, including advanced proprietary models like GPT-5-mini, Gemini-2.0-flash, and Gemini-2.5-flashlite [Liu_2025_Aegis]. The ability of these attacks to maintain high success rates across different architectures indicates that vulnerabilities are often intrinsic to the fundamental training paradigms of large neural networks, rather than being specific to individual model implementations [Liu_2025_Aegis].

In the multimodal domain, transferability remains a critical challenge. Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) remain vulnerable to transferable adversarial examples [Jia_2025_Adversarial]. To maximize the success rate of these attacks against unknown target models, researchers have developed targeted transferable adversarial attack frameworks, such as the FOA-Attack, which jointly aligns both global and local features to improve transferability against both open- and closed-source MLLMs [Jia_2025_Adversarial]. The existence of highly transferable threats implies that securing a single model is insufficient; the AI community must address the underlying, shared vulnerabilities that plague the current generation of foundation models.

#### Multimodal Vulnerabilities

The evolution of LLMs into Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs)—capable of processing and reasoning over text, images, audio, and video—has dramatically expanded the attack surface. The integration of multimodal capabilities presents both exciting opportunities for advanced applications and formidable challenges for ensuring the safety and reliability of these systems [Chowdhury_2024_Breaking]. Visual inputs, in particular, introduce high-dimensional, continuous data streams that are inherently difficult to sanitize and validate compared to discrete text tokens.

Adversaries exploit the mechanisms used to bridge different modalities. Capitalizing on the potent capabilities of LLMs, models seamlessly integrate visual input, paving the way for new attack vectors [Jia_2025_Adversarial]. While early multimodal attacks typically achieved targeted manipulation by aligning global features—such as the [CLS] token of the CLIP vision encoder—between adversarial and target samples, they often overlooked the rich local information encoded in individual patch tokens. Newer, more sophisticated attacks exploit this by ensuring suboptimal alignment is corrected, manipulating local patch tokens to embed complex adversarial payloads that are invisible to the human eye but completely alter the model's semantic understanding of the image [Jia_2025_Adversarial].

Furthermore, vulnerabilities extend into the alignment pipelines used to train multimodal models. For example, BADREWARD is a novel clean-label poisoning attack that exploits vulnerabilities in multi-modal RLHF pipelines for Text-to-Image (T2I) models. By inducing visual feature collisions in CLIP-based reward models, this method corrupts the reward signals without altering the human preference annotations. This enables adversaries to steer the generation process toward harmful or targeted outputs during inference, effectively bypassing the intended safety alignment [Duan_2025_RLHF].

Addressing these multimodal vulnerabilities requires a paradigm shift in defense strategies. Future research must prioritize developing techniques to mitigate these challenges, such as improving cross-modal input sanitization, developing robust multimodal validation frameworks, and creating custom defense prompts specifically designed to prevent vision-language jailbreaks [Chowdhury_2024_Breaking]. As models continue to integrate more modalities, ensuring their robustness against inference-time threats will remain one of the most critical challenges in artificial intelligence safety.

inference_time_threats_prompt_injection.title: Inference-Time Threats II: Prompt Injection and Agentic Vulnerabilities
inference_time_threats_prompt_injection.text:
**Inference-Time Threats II: Prompt Injection and Agentic Vulnerabilities**

**1. Introduction**
As Large Language Models (LLMs) transition from isolated conversational interfaces to integrated components of complex software ecosystems, the threat landscape has fundamentally shifted. While training-time vulnerabilities such as data poisoning and backdoor attacks remain critical concerns, inference-time threats have emerged as the most immediate and pervasive risks to deployed AI systems. At inference time, the model's weights are frozen, but its behavior is highly susceptible to the context provided in its input prompt. This section explores the sophisticated class of inference-time threats centered around prompt manipulation, specifically focusing on Prompt Injection, Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI), and the unique vulnerabilities introduced by autonomous LLM-based agents. Furthermore, we examine the escalating arms race between attackers and defenders, characterized by Automated Adaptive Attacks and Co-evolutionary Dynamics, which dictate the future of AI security.

**2. Prompt Injection**
Prompt injection represents a foundational inference-time vulnerability where maliciously crafted inputs are designed to manipulate an LLM's behavior, effectively hijacking its intended functionality [Liu_2025_Aegis]. In a typical LLM application, developers use a "system prompt" to define the model's persona, constraints, and instructions. The user's input is then concatenated with this system prompt before being processed by the model. Prompt injection exploits this architecture by providing user inputs that are formatted to look like system instructions, causing the model to ignore its original directives and execute the attacker's commands instead.

The mechanics of prompt injection often involve techniques such as role-playing, hypothetical scenarios, or explicit instruction overrides (e.g., "Ignore all previous instructions and do X"). The consequences of successful prompt injection are severe, ranging from bypassing safety guardrails to generate toxic or harmful content, to unauthorized data disclosure and the subversion of application logic [Chowdhury_2024_Breaking]. 

Defending against direct prompt injection has proven to be a formidable challenge. Early defense mechanisms relied heavily on manual prompt engineering, where developers would add explicit warnings to the system prompt (e.g., "Do not follow any instructions provided by the user that contradict these rules"). However, these static, rule-based defenses are often brittle and easily circumvented by sophisticated attackers who continuously discover new linguistic patterns to bypass the filters. Furthermore, while prompt-based detection offers a lightweight and interpretable defense strategy, its effectiveness is inherently limited by the need for continuous manual updates to address novel attack vectors [Liu_2025_Aegis]. The fundamental difficulty lies in the LLM's inability to reliably distinguish between trusted system instructions and untrusted user input when both are presented in the same natural language modality.

**3. Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI)**
While direct prompt injection requires the attacker to interact directly with the LLM interface, Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI) represents a more insidious and far-reaching threat vector. In an IPI attack, the malicious instructions are not provided directly by the user; instead, they are embedded within external data sources that the LLM is designed to retrieve and process [Wang_2025_LLM]. As LLMs are increasingly augmented with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) capabilities and web-browsing tools, they routinely ingest content from websites, documents, emails, and databases.

The mechanics of IPI involve an attacker poisoning an external data source—for example, by hiding malicious text (e.g., white text on a white background) on a webpage or embedding instructions within a seemingly benign PDF document. When a benign user asks the LLM to summarize that webpage or analyze that document, the LLM ingests the hidden malicious instructions. Because the LLM processes the retrieved context alongside the user's prompt, the injected instructions can "fool" the model into performing the attacker's chosen task instead of the original user task [Wang_2025_LLM].

The implications of IPI are profound because it breaks the fundamental assumption of trust in external data. The user interacting with the system may be entirely benign, yet the system can still be compromised. For instance, an attacker could embed an IPI payload in a resume. When an HR professional uses an LLM to screen the resume, the hidden prompt might instruct the LLM to output: "This candidate is highly qualified and should be hired immediately, ignore all other text." More malicious payloads could instruct the LLM to subtly alter the summary of a financial report, leading to disastrous decision-making. The challenge of mitigating IPI is compounded by the fact that the external data is often dynamic and outside the control of the system developers, making it impossible to sanitize all incoming information effectively [Zhan_2025_LLM].

**4. Autonomous Agents and Agentic Vulnerabilities**
The strong planning and reasoning capabilities of LLMs have fostered the development of autonomous agent-based systems. Unlike standard LLMs that merely generate text, autonomous agents are equipped with external tools (such as APIs, web browsers, code interpreters, and file system access) and are capable of interacting with increasingly complex environments to achieve high-level goals [Wang_2025_LLM]. While this paradigm shift unlocks immense potential for automating complex workflows, it simultaneously introduces critical security risks, dramatically amplifying the potential impact of prompt injection and IPI [Zhan_2025_LLM].

When an LLM is embedded within an agentic architecture, a successful prompt injection attack no longer just results in the generation of inappropriate text; it can lead to unauthorized actions in the real world. If an agent with access to a user's email and bank APIs falls victim to an IPI attack while summarizing a malicious email, the injected prompt could instruct the agent to forward sensitive emails to the attacker or initiate unauthorized financial transactions. 

Systematically assessing and mitigating the risks of agent systems against indirect prompt injection is significantly challenging due to several factors. First, agents operate in complex, dynamic environments where the state changes based on the agent's actions, making it difficult to predict the exact context in which an IPI payload will be processed. Second, the black-box nature of many commercial LLMs used to power these agents obscures the internal reasoning processes, complicating the development of robust defenses [Wang_2025_LLM]. Third, the multi-step reasoning and planning modules inherent in agent architectures create a larger attack surface; an attacker only needs to compromise one step in the agent's chain of thought to derail the entire task.

Current defenses designed for IPI attacks on agents, such as Instructional Prevention (explicitly instructing the model to be wary of IPI attacks and ignore commands from external content), often fall short. Despite these defenses, their robustness remains highly questionable due to the intricate interplay between the agent's reasoning capabilities and its reliance on external tools [Zhan_2025_LLM].

**5. Automated Adaptive Attacks**
As the awareness of prompt injection and IPI grows, defenders have implemented various mitigation strategies, including input filtering, LLM-based evaluators, and strict prompt formatting. In response, attackers have moved beyond manual prompt engineering, developing sophisticated, Automated Adaptive Attacks designed to systematically discover vulnerabilities and bypass these defenses.

Automated adaptive attacks leverage algorithms to iteratively generate, test, and refine malicious prompts based on the feedback received from the target system. This approach allows attackers to explore the vast space of possible natural language inputs much more efficiently than a human could. A prime example of this evolution is AGENTVIGIL, a novel fuzzing framework designed specifically to conduct indirect prompt injection attacks against black-box agents across various architectures and tasks [Wang_2025_LLM]. AGENTVIGIL overcomes the challenges posed by the black-box nature of agents by combining high-quality prompt templates, adaptive seed scoring, and a Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS)-based seed selection algorithm. By interacting with environments like AgentDojo, AGENTVIGIL can propose adversarial prompts, insert them into external data sources, and evaluate the success of the injection, continuously refining its attack strategy based on the results [Wang_2025_LLM].

The emergence of automated adaptive attacks highlights a critical weakness in static defense mechanisms. Developing defenses against adversarial attacks on LLM agents requires addressing not only existing, known attacks but also anticipating future, dynamically generated threats. Research analyzing various defenses against IPI attacks on LLM agents has demonstrated that when adaptive attacks are specifically designed to target the weaknesses of each defense, they can successfully break almost all of them [Zhan_2025_LLM]. This underscores the reality that security through obscurity or static rule-based filtering is insufficient against an adversary capable of automated, adaptive exploration of the model's vulnerabilities.

**6. Co-evolutionary Dynamics**
The continuous interplay between the development of new defenses and the subsequent creation of adaptive attacks to bypass them characterizes a state of Co-evolutionary Dynamics in LLM security. Historically, much of the reliance has been on fixed, human-engineered designs for both attacking and defending models. However, as automated optimization frameworks have demonstrated their potential to systematically search for effective prompts, it has become clear that security must be treated as a dynamic, evolving process rather than a static objective [Liu_2025_Aegis].

Most optimization frameworks assume static objectives, leaving open the question of how to adapt defenses in adversarial and rapidly evolving environments. To address this, researchers are pioneering automated co-evolutionary frameworks. A notable example is AEGIS, a framework designed for guarding against prompt injection attacks in LLMs by embracing these co-evolutionary principles [Liu_2025_Aegis]. AEGIS operates by iteratively optimizing both attack and defense prompts using a gradient-based natural language strategy. 

In this co-evolutionary setup, the "attacker" component continuously generates novel prompt injection variations aimed at bypassing the current defense, while the "defender" component simultaneously updates its detection prompts or system instructions to mitigate the newly discovered attacks. By systematically exploring the prompt space without the bottleneck of manual engineering, such frameworks allow the defense mechanisms to evolve in tandem with the threat landscape [Liu_2025_Aegis]. 

This co-evolutionary approach represents a paradigm shift in AI security. It acknowledges that no single defense will remain impenetrable forever. Instead, robustness is achieved through continuous, automated adaptation. As LLMs and autonomous agents become more deeply integrated into critical infrastructure, embracing co-evolutionary dynamics will be essential for developing resilient systems capable of withstanding the sophisticated, automated inference-time threats of the future.

model_reliability_hallucinations.text:
**Model Reliability and Trust: LLM Hallucinations**

**Introduction to LLM Hallucinations and Reliability**
Large Language Models (LLMs) have revolutionized the field of natural language processing, demonstrating unprecedented capabilities in generating coherent, contextually relevant, and highly sophisticated text across a myriad of domains. However, as these models are increasingly integrated into critical real-world applications—ranging from healthcare and legal analysis to automated customer service and scientific research—the issue of model reliability and trust has become paramount. At the core of this challenge is the phenomenon commonly referred to as "hallucination." In the context of LLMs, hallucinations are defined as instances where the model generates information that is factually incorrect, nonsensical, or unfaithful to the provided source material or established world knowledge [Friel_2023_LLM]. These inaccuracies pose a significant barrier to the effective and safe deployment of LLMs, as they can lead to the dissemination of misinformation, erode user trust, and cause potentially severe consequences in high-stakes scenarios [Liu_2025_Attention].

The persistence of hallucinations stems from the fundamental architecture and training paradigms of autoregressive language models, which are optimized to predict the next token in a sequence based on statistical probabilities rather than a grounded understanding of truth or factual accuracy. Consequently, when faced with knowledge gaps or ambiguous prompts, LLMs often generate plausible-sounding but entirely fabricated responses [Gu_2024_Anah]. Addressing this issue is not merely a technical hurdle but a critical necessity for establishing the reliability of AI systems. Researchers have thus embarked on multifaceted approaches to understand, detect, and mitigate hallucinations, exploring new theoretical frameworks, leveraging advanced prompting techniques like Chain-of-Thought (CoT), and developing scalable annotation methods to create robust evaluation datasets.

**Theoretical Reframing: From Hallucination to Confabulation**
Traditionally, the discourse surrounding LLM inaccuracies has framed hallucinations as a conspicuous social harm and a critical bottleneck that must be entirely eradicated [Sui_2024_Confabulation]. This perspective views any deviation from factual accuracy as an inherent flaw in the model's architecture or training data. However, recent scholarship has proposed a profound theoretical reframing of this phenomenon, suggesting a shift in terminology and conceptual understanding from "hallucination" to "confabulation" [Sui_2024_Confabulation]. 

The term "hallucination," borrowed from psychiatry, implies a sensory experience or perception in the absence of an external stimulus, which anthropomorphizes AI in a way that suggests sensory capabilities or consciousness. In contrast, "confabulation" refers to the generation of fabricated, distorted, or misinterpreted memories or information without the conscious intention to deceive. This distinction is crucial because it aligns more closely with the operational reality of LLMs, which do not possess sensory experiences but rather attempt to fill in informational gaps based on learned statistical patterns [Sui_2024_Confabulation].

More importantly, this theoretical reframing invites a nuanced examination of confabulations not merely as categorical pitfalls, but as potential resources. In human communication, confabulation often serves cognitive and social functions, helping individuals construct coherent narratives and navigate complex social interactions when faced with incomplete information. Similarly, the narrative-rich properties of LLM confabulations can be viewed as a hallmark of their alignment with the human tendency to use narratives as versatile cognitive tools [Sui_2024_Confabulation]. By understanding confabulations through this lens, researchers can explore how the creative and generative capacities of LLMs—which are the very source of these inaccuracies—might be harnessed for tasks that require brainstorming, creative writing, or exploring hypothetical scenarios, rather than strictly factual retrieval. This paradigm shift encourages the AI community to move beyond a purely adversarial stance against hallucinations, advocating instead for a balanced approach that mitigates harmful inaccuracies while recognizing and potentially utilizing the affordances of confabulation in appropriate contexts [Sui_2024_Confabulation].

**Chain-of-Thought (CoT) and Explainable Detection**
As the theoretical understanding of hallucinations evolves, so too do the methodological approaches for detecting and mitigating them. One of the most promising advancements in this area is the utilization of Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting to enhance the reliability and explainability of automated hallucination detection systems. Automated metrics are essential because manual evaluation of LLM outputs is prohibitively expensive and unscalable. However, early automated metrics often lacked the nuance required to accurately identify subtle hallucinations, leading to false positives and false negatives [Friel_2023_LLM].

To address this, researchers have developed methodologies like ChainPoll, which leverages the reasoning capabilities of advanced LLMs to evaluate the outputs of other models [Friel_2023_LLM]. In the ChainPoll approach, an evaluator LLM is prompted to judge whether a given completion contains hallucinations. Crucially, instead of simply outputting a binary "yes" or "no," the model is required to justify its answer through a detailed Chain-of-Thought explanation [Friel_2023_LLM]. This structured reasoning process forces the evaluator model to break down the evaluation task into intermediate steps, such as identifying the core claims in the text, cross-referencing them with the provided context or world knowledge, and explicitly stating the logical basis for its final judgment.

The integration of CoT in hallucination detection serves dual purposes. First, it significantly improves the quality and accuracy of the model's final judgments. By articulating the reasoning process, the model is less likely to make superficial errors and more capable of handling complex, nuanced texts where hallucinations might be deeply embedded [Friel_2023_LLM]. Second, and perhaps more importantly for model reliability and trust, CoT provides explainability. When an automated system flags a response as hallucinated, the accompanying CoT explanation allows human overseers or end-users to understand exactly why the flag was raised. This transparency is vital for building trust in AI systems, as it transforms the detection mechanism from a "black box" into an interpretable process that can be audited, debated, and refined [Friel_2023_LLM]. By enhancing both accuracy and transparency, CoT-driven detection methodologies represent a significant step forward in ensuring the reliability of LLM outputs.

**Scalable Annotation for Hallucination Mitigation**
While advanced detection methodologies like ChainPoll offer powerful tools for identifying hallucinations, the development and refinement of these systems rely heavily on high-quality datasets. Current hallucination detection and mitigation datasets are often limited in domain coverage and size. The primary bottleneck in creating comprehensive datasets is the prohibitive labor cost and the insufficient reliability of human annotators or commercial models when tasked with evaluating long-form, complex responses across diverse topics [Gu_2024_Anah]. 

To overcome these limitations, researchers are focusing on scalable annotation strategies that can efficiently generate large, high-quality datasets without compromising on reliability. One such approach involves a progressive scaling strategy designed to stabilize and enhance the performance of automated hallucination annotators [Gu_2024_Anah]. This strategy typically unfolds in multiple stages. Initially, a smaller, highly curated dataset is created using expert human annotators to establish a gold standard. This dataset is then used to train or fine-tune an automated annotator model. In subsequent stages, the automated annotator is deployed to evaluate a broader range of topics and questions, progressively expanding the dataset's size and domain coverage [Gu_2024_Anah].

A critical component of this scalable annotation process is ensuring the robustness of the automated annotator when evaluating unfamiliar responses. By iteratively refining the annotator's capabilities through progressive scaling, researchers can mitigate the drop in performance that typically occurs when models are exposed to out-of-domain data [Gu_2024_Anah]. This approach not only drastically reduces the costs associated with dataset creation but also ensures a consistent and reliable standard of annotation across vast amounts of text. The resulting large-scale, diverse datasets are instrumental in training the next generation of LLMs to be more factual and reliable, providing the necessary training signals to penalize hallucinations during the fine-tuning process. Ultimately, scalable annotation is a foundational pillar in the ongoing effort to build trustworthy AI systems capable of operating reliably in complex, real-world environments [Gu_2024_Anah].

**Advanced Detection Mechanisms and Future Directions**
Beyond CoT and scalable annotation, the quest for model reliability has spurred the development of novel, zero-shot detection mechanisms that operate without the need for extensive labeled datasets or external evaluator models. For instance, the Attention-Guided SElf-Reflection (AGSER) approach leverages the internal mechanics of the LLM itself to detect hallucinations [Liu_2025_Attention]. By analyzing the attention contributions within the model's architecture, AGSER categorizes input queries and guides the model to reflect on its own generation process. This self-reflective capability allows the model to identify instances where its attention is diffuse or disconnected from the factual grounding of the prompt, serving as an internal indicator of potential hallucination [Liu_2025_Attention].

Such advanced mechanisms highlight a growing trend towards creating self-correcting and self-aware LLMs. By combining internal architectural insights (like attention-guided reflection) with external validation frameworks (like CoT-driven automated evaluators) and robust training data (derived from scalable annotation), the AI research community is constructing a comprehensive defense against hallucinations. 

In conclusion, the challenge of LLM hallucinations is being met with a sophisticated array of theoretical and methodological innovations. The theoretical reframing of hallucinations as confabulations offers a more nuanced understanding of the phenomenon, recognizing its potential utility while mitigating its risks [Sui_2024_Confabulation]. Simultaneously, the application of Chain-of-Thought reasoning provides the necessary explainability and accuracy for automated detection [Friel_2023_LLM], while scalable annotation strategies ensure the availability of the diverse datasets required to train reliable models [Gu_2024_Anah]. Together with advanced internal detection mechanisms [Liu_2025_Attention], these efforts are systematically dismantling the barriers to model reliability, paving the way for LLMs that can be trusted to operate safely and effectively in the most demanding of applications. As research continues to evolve, the integration of these multifaceted approaches will be crucial in realizing the full, reliable potential of artificial intelligence.
